Iowa State enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 27-7 overall and 12-6 in Big 12 play, with a Friday, March 20, 2026 first-round game against Tennessee State after reaching the Big 12 Tournament semifinals. The official Iowa State cumulative stat report lists the Cyclones at 27-7 through March 13, 2026, and the Big 12-only page confirms the 12-6 league mark. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Offensively, this is still a traditional Otzelberger team in one key sense: the offense runs through decision-making guards and physical forwards rather than pure pace-and-space volume. The hard numbers show the structure. Joshua Jefferson leads the team with 167 assists from the frontcourt, Tamin Lipsey has 156 assists at point, and Iowa State gets interior efficiency from Blake Buchanan at 64.5 percent from the field. Milan Momcilovic is the spacing piece who warps the floor; he has 127 made threes at 49.6 percent, the clearest proof that Iowa State’s half-court offense is built around drive-kick action into trail and slot threes for him. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Specific tendencies show up in game recaps. Against Arizona State on March 7, Iowa State trailed 41-37 at halftime, then ripped off a 24-0 second-half run. In that stretch, Momcilovic hit two threes and Jefferson scored six points, while Lipsey’s ball pressure created transition chances. That is a named example of Iowa State’s favorite offensive sequence: defensive stop, advance, paint touch, kickout three or early-clock attack before the defense resets. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-no-6-iowa-state-comes-alive-in-second-half-in-86-65-win-vs-arizona-state))

Another concrete example came February 24 at Utah in a 75-59 win. Iowa State’s own recap says the offense “dominated the paint” behind Joshua Jefferson, while Momcilovic broke the school single-season three-point record in the same game. That combination is the scouting report in one sentence: Jefferson works as a face-up driver, post isolator, and short-roll passer; Momcilovic is the designated movement-and-catch shooter who punishes help. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/news/2026/2/24/mens-basketball-momcilovic-makes-history-in-road-win-over-utah?utm_source=openai))

Defensively, Iowa State remains built on ball pressure, deflections, and turnover creation. The March 7 Arizona State game is the cleanest example: the Cyclones forced 23 Sun Devil turnovers, including eight in the first eight minutes of the second half. Four days later, in the Big 12 Tournament opener against the same opponent, Iowa State forced 23 more turnovers in a 91-42 win, and the school noted that 46 combined turnovers were forced across the two meetings. That is not generic “good defense”; it is a specific, repeatable identity based on pressure at the point of attack, loaded help behind it, and converting mistakes into immediate scoring runs. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-no-6-iowa-state-comes-alive-in-second-half-in-86-65-win-vs-arizona-state))

The philosophy is also visible in losses. At Arizona on March 2, Iowa State lost 73-57 despite forcing more turnovers than it committed and scoring 16 points off giveaways, because Arizona won the glass 40-33 and held ISU to only 16 points in the paint, well below Iowa State’s 38.0 season average in the lane. That game showed the counter to Iowa State’s style: if an opponent handles the first wave of pressure and keeps ISU out of the paint, the Cyclones can become jump-shot dependent. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/news/2026/3/2/mens-basketball-isu-falls-in-top-10-bout-at-arizona))

T.J. Otzelberger’s coaching philosophy is documented by how quickly his team changes coverage intensity and lineup emphasis inside games. The March 7 Arizona State game is a direct adjustment example: after a sloppy close to the first half with five turnovers in the final three minutes, Iowa State came out after halftime and immediately turned the game with full-force pressure, producing the 24-0 run. Against No. 2 Houston on February 16, Iowa State trailed by 10 with seven minutes left, then closed on a 17-4 run to win 70-67, with Nate Heise and Jamarion Batemon making decisive late plays. That is classic Otzelberger: shorten the game, trust toughness, and change tempo through defense rather than through wholesale offensive experimentation. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-no-6-iowa-state-comes-alive-in-second-half-in-86-65-win-vs-arizona-state))

Late-game execution is good enough to matter in March, but not flawless. The best clutch win is the February 16, 2026 home win over No. 2 Houston, 70-67. Iowa State was down 10 with 7:00 left and finished the game on a 17-4 run. Another example is the Big 12 semifinal on March 13, when Iowa State lost 82-80 to No. 2 Arizona at the buzzer after Momcilovic hit three threes in the final 30 seconds of the first half and the Cyclones still had a chance to steal the game late. The March 13 loss matters because it showed both sides: Iowa State can generate shotmaking under pressure, but it can still be beaten in final-possession situations by elite creators. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/news/2026/2/16/mens-basketball-no-2-houston-falls-to-no-6-iowa-state-hilton-magic-70-67?utm_source=openai))

Key players start with Momcilovic, the primary scorer at 17.1 points per game. He is shooting 51.2 percent from the field, 49.6 percent from three, and 88.0 percent at the line. His recent form is elite: he scored 24 against Syracuse on November 26 with six made threes, had 20 against Texas Tech on February 28, and authored the three-triple burst late in the first half against Arizona on March 13. He is the half-court matchup problem because he can score in pindown-style catches, spot-ups, and quick pick-and-pop actions. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Jefferson is the engine piece at 16.9 points, 7.6 rebounds, and 167 assists. His value is traditional scouting gold because he fills every column: rebounding, facilitation, late-clock drives, and foul drawing. Against Syracuse, he had 13 points, six rebounds, and a career-high 10 assists with zero turnovers. Against Texas Tech on February 28, he scored 22. At Utah on February 24, Iowa State’s recap explicitly tied the paint offense to his “monster performance.” He is the player most likely to control a tournament game without leading in scoring. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Lipsey is the tone-setter: 13.3 points, 156 assists, and 68 steals in 31 games. On Senior Day against Arizona State on March 7, he had 16 points, six assists, and a season-high six steals. Iowa State’s defensive personality starts with him at the point of attack. If his pressure is disrupting rhythm, the whole defense tightens. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Buchanan gives them a true interior finisher and screener: 8.4 points, 5.7 rebounds, and 64.5 percent shooting. Killyan Toure adds 8.1 points, 74 assists, and 49 steals as a secondary creator/defender. Jamarion Batemon is the bench change-up guard at 6.9 points and 38.9 percent from three; he made the momentum-starting three in the Houston comeback and scored 14 at Arizona. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Notable wins: Houston on February 16, 70-67, revealed Iowa State can win a rock fight against a national-title-level opponent; Arizona State on March 11, 91-42, showed the ceiling of its turnover-forcing defense; Texas Tech on March 12, 75-53, showed how dangerous Iowa State is when it can turn a ranked opponent into a half-court survival game; Syracuse on November 26, 95-64, showed offensive balance, with five double-figure scorers and Jefferson’s 10-assist, zero-turnover line. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/news/2026/2/16/mens-basketball-no-2-houston-falls-to-no-6-iowa-state-hilton-magic-70-67?utm_source=openai))

Notable losses: Kansas on January 13, 84-63, exposed Iowa State’s vulnerability in hostile environments when turnovers pile up early; BYU on February 21, 79-69, reinforced that road shotmaking can waver; Arizona on March 2, 73-57, showed that if opponents win the glass and keep ISU to 16 paint points, the offense can bog down; Arizona again on March 13, 82-80, showed Iowa State is close to the elite tier but still can lose the final-possession battle. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/news/2026/1/13/mens-basketball-no-2-cyclones-upended-at-kansas-suffer-first-loss-of-season?utm_source=openai))

As for Otzelberger’s NCAA tournament history as a head coach, Iowa State’s official bio lists six NCAA trips overall as a head coach and four at Iowa State through 2025. At South Dakota State, he reached the NCAA first round in 2017 and 2018. At Iowa State, he reached the Sweet 16 in 2022, the first round in 2023, the Sweet 16 in 2024, and the second round in 2025. Iowa State’s official site also notes he became the first coach in school history to take the program to multiple Sweet 16s, specifically in 2022 and 2024. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/coaches/t-j-otzelberger/2378))

Bottom line: Iowa State is a legitimate second-weekend threat because its defense is not theoretical; it has produced named turnover avalanches against Arizona State, a comeback win over Houston, and a 75-53 demolition of Texas Tech. The risk is equally concrete: Kansas beat it 84-63, Arizona beat it twice in March, and when the Cyclones do not win the paint or the turnover battle decisively, the offense can flatten into difficult jump shooting. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/news/2026/3/11/mens-basketball-cyclones-crush-sun-devils-in-historic-big-12-tournament-win))

Iowa State enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with one of the cleaner high-end statistical résumés in the field: elite predictive rankings, a strong win-loss profile, plus a team-stat base that supports the idea that this is a genuine contender rather than a paper tiger. As of March 10, 2026, Warren Nolan’s comparison page had the Cyclones at No. 8 in NET, No. 12 in BPI, No. 7 in KenPom/Pomeroy, and No. 9 in Bart Torvik’s T-Rank. A separate KenPom-derived ranking snapshot listed Iowa State No. 6 nationally, with the 21st-ranked offense and 4th-ranked defense. Taken together, that puts the Cyclones squarely in the national top tier, but with a profile driven a bit more by defense and two-way balance than by overwhelming offensive dominance. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings?utm_source=openai))

The raw season numbers through March 13, 2026 are excellent. Iowa State was 27-7 overall and 12-6 in Big 12 play, with a 16-1 home record, 5-5 road record, and 6-1 on neutral floors. The Cyclones scored 81.8 points per game and allowed just 65.1, a +16.6 scoring margin. They shot 49.0 percent from the field, 38.7 percent from three, and held opponents to 42.6 percent overall and 32.1 percent from deep. They also forced 15.3 opponent turnovers per game while committing only 10.3 themselves, giving them a very strong +5.0 turnover margin. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Using the official season totals, Iowa State’s possession-based offensive shape is also strong. Their team effective field-goal percentage computes to 56.47 percent, turnover percentage to 12.91 percent, offensive rebounding percentage to 35.32 percent, free-throw rate to 33.98 percent, and three-point attempt rate to 38.77 percent. That is a highly modern, analytically friendly mix: they shoot efficiently, rarely waste possessions, rebound their misses at a strong clip, and take a healthy volume of threes without becoming wholly dependent on them. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Their raw efficiency estimates from the full-season box-score data come out to roughly 125.1 points scored and 99.7 points allowed per 100 possessions using a simple pace estimate based on FGA and FTA, or about 104.7 scored and 83.4 allowed per 100 using the more standard turnover-inclusive possession estimate. The exact adjusted numbers are not openly available from KenPom in the retrieved sources, but the directional takeaway is clear from the ranking splits: Iowa State is operating like a top-10 team overall, with a defense that grades as elite and an offense that is very good but not quite at the absolute apex of the sport. ([cleatz.com](https://cleatz.com/latest-kenpom-rankings/))

Pace-wise, Iowa State does not read like a pure track-meet team despite the gaudy scoring average. Based on season totals, their estimated tempo lands in the mid-60s possessions per game, which suggests a moderate pace rather than an extreme one. That matters because the offense is getting to 81.8 points not by simply playing recklessly fast, but by being efficient, taking care of the ball, and generating quality half-court offense plus turnover-fueled extra possessions. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

The personnel numbers explain a lot. Milan Momcilovic has been the offensive ceiling-raiser: 17.1 points per game, 51.2 percent from the floor, and a staggering 49.6 percent on 127-of-256 three-point shooting. Joshua Jefferson adds 16.9 points, 7.6 rebounds, and 167 assists, giving the Cyclones a playmaking forward who fills every column. Tamin Lipsey contributes 13.3 points and 156 assists against only 45 turnovers, continuing to serve as the backcourt stabilizer. RotoWire went so far as to describe Momcilovic as the nation’s best three-point shooter, and even if that label is a little loose, the percentage is real and completely changes Iowa State’s spacing geometry. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Strength of schedule is strong, though not at the absolute top of the field. Warren Nolan’s NET SOS board listed Iowa State No. 28 nationally, with a non-conference SOS of 129. That profile fits what the game log shows: quality non-league wins over Purdue, St. John’s, Creighton, Syracuse, Mississippi State, and Iowa, then a difficult Big 12 grind that included wins over Kansas, Houston, Baylor twice, and road wins at Baylor, Kansas State, Oklahoma State, and Utah. Iowa State also owned six Quadrant 1 wins and a 66.7 percent Q1 win rate in one Warren Nolan snapshot. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/sos-net))

The recent-form story is more nuanced than the season-long résumé. Iowa State closed the regular season with some slippage, losing four of its final seven regular-season games and showing offensive regression. A March 2026 report citing Bart Torvik noted that Iowa State’s offensive efficiency over the previous 10 games had fallen to 121.3, just 46th nationally over that span. That aligns with the eye test from the late-season log: losses to TCU, BYU, Texas Tech, and Arizona all came in a roughly three-week window, and the offense dipped below its season norms in several of those games. ([si.com](https://www.si.com/college/iowa-state/latest-news/iowa-state-cyclones-have-seen-steady-decline-in-this-key-area))

At the same time, the Big 12 tournament reminded everyone why the predictive systems still love this team. Iowa State smashed Arizona State 91-42 and Texas Tech 75-53 before losing a tight 82-80 final to Arizona. So the most honest tournament read is that the Cyclones were not trending like a dominant juggernaut, but neither were they collapsing; rather, they were oscillating between merely good offense and top-five-level defense, with enough shooting and ball security to quickly look overwhelming again. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/isuni.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

This is where the numbers diverge a bit from conventional wisdom. The casual read on Iowa State is often “defense-first, grind-you-down Big 12 team.” That is only half right. The defense is indeed the identity anchor; KenPom-derived splits had them 4th nationally on defense. But the offensive profile is much more explosive than the stereotype suggests: 81.8 points per game, 38.7 percent from three, 56.5 percent eFG, a sub-13 percent turnover rate, and a near-39 percent three-point attempt rate. The bigger hidden weakness is not scoring creativity; it is free-throw shooting. RotoWire notes Iowa State ranks 340th nationally at 67.2 percent from the line, and the official team totals confirm the same 67.2 percent mark. That is a real March vulnerability in coin-flip games. ([cleatz.com](https://cleatz.com/latest-kenpom-rankings/))

Bottom line: Iowa State’s 2026 profile is that of a legitimate second-weekend-or-better team with top-10 predictive strength, elite defensive credibility, strong shooting efficiency, excellent turnover control, and enough résumé substance to justify trust. The caution flags are a merely good rather than dominant offense by adjusted standards, some late-season offensive fade, and poor foul shooting. But the aggregate statistical picture is still extremely favorable: this is a balanced, physical, efficient team whose defense gives it a high floor and whose shotmaking gives it a championship-caliber ceiling. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings?utm_source=openai))
matchup-analyst:
Iowa State enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a 26-6 record and a top-tier profile built on ball pressure, low-turnover offense, versatile forwards, and efficient half-court execution. Publicly available 2025-26 team stats list the Cyclones at 82.1 points per game, 48.9% from the field, 17.4 assists per game, only 9.9 turnovers per game, and 9.0 steals per game, with a 122.3 offensive rating and 96.9 defensive rating. Their roster is old and big on the wings: Tamin Lipsey is a 6-1 senior lead guard, Killyan Toure a 6-3 freshman combo guard, Nate Heise and Dominick Nelson are both 6-5 wings, Milan Momcilovic is a 6-8 junior forward, Joshua Jefferson is a 6-9 senior forward, Blake Buchanan is a 6-10 junior big, and Dominykas Pleta gives them a 6-11 reserve frontcourt body. That size map matters because Iowa State can play effectively 1-through-4 with plus length without sacrificing skill. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/2025-26))

Style-wise, Iowa State wants to win with disruptive perimeter defense flowing into organized offense rather than pure chaos. The giveaway is the combination of 9.0 steals per game with just 9.9 turnovers committed per game: they pressure you more than they self-destruct. Offensively, they are not a pure isolation team; the 17.4 assists per game and strong assist/turnover profile show a team that prefers advantage creation through paint touches, drive-and-kick, and frontcourt facilitation. Joshua Jefferson is the key connector because at 6-9 he functions as a mismatch forward who can score, pass, and trigger offense from the elbows or after defensive rebounds. In the 70-67 win over Houston on February 16, 2026, Iowa State got assisted makes from Jefferson to Toure, Heise, and Buchanan, and won a grinder despite Houston’s pressure by staying organized late. That is the template: force turnovers, keep their own low, then let Jefferson/Lipsey/Momcilovic make the next read. ([foxsports.com](https://www.foxsports.com/college-basketball/iowa-state-cyclones-team-stats?utm_source=openai))

What disrupts that style? First, physical rim pressure from bigger scoring wings. In BYU’s 79-69 win on February 21, 2026, AJ Dybantsa went for 29 points, 10 rebounds, and nine assists, and BYU attacked the rim early, outscoring Iowa State 22-6 in the paint in the first half. That is not random noise; it is evidence that Iowa State’s pressure can be neutralized if a jumbo creator beats the first line and forces rotation. Second, elite rebounding/paint volume can blunt their steal edge. The 2025 BYU win in Ames is older evidence, but it is still stylistically relevant: BYU survived 29 turnovers and still won because it dominated the glass 52-24. Even when Iowa State’s pressure lands, they can still be vulnerable if the opponent is bigger, plays through contact, and turns the game into a finishing/rebounding contest instead of a passing-lane contest. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401827693))

Press vulnerability: there is not strong evidence that Iowa State itself is notably weak against pressure; in fact, the opposite is more supportable. The season-long 9.9 turnovers per game and their win over Houston, one of the nation’s most physical defensive teams, point to relative press resistance. In that Houston game, Iowa State closed possessions with half-court execution and enough secondary playmaking from Jefferson, Lipsey, and Toure to avoid getting sped into collapse. So if you press Iowa State, it has to be selective and after makes; full-game reckless pressure is unlikely to work unless you also have length on the back line to take away reversal passes and diagonal outlets. ([foxsports.com](https://www.foxsports.com/college-basketball/iowa-state-cyclones-team-stats?utm_source=openai))

Zone vulnerability is more plausible than press vulnerability, but only in a specific form: long, active matchup zone that takes away middle catches and runs Momcilovic off clean catch-and-shoot rhythm. Iowa State’s offense is efficient overall, but much of its clean spacing depends on Momcilovic as a floor-bender and on Jefferson as the short-roll/high-post decision-maker. When opponents keep them out of the paint first, the offense can become more shotmaking-dependent. BYU’s February 21 win is again useful indirect evidence because BYU forced Iowa State into a lower-output 69-point game while winning the paint decisively; that is the blueprint even if the coverages were mixed. There is not enough public game-log evidence to claim a specific repeated zone failure, so the safer scouting conclusion is: zone them only if your length can erase the high post and your closeouts can get to Momcilovic. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401827693))

Preferred pace: Iowa State is most dangerous in controlled, efficient possessions rather than a pure track meet. Their profile of high efficiency, low turnovers, and high steals says they prefer a game where they create extra possessions without playing reckless tempo. To force the opposite, you either make them guard deep into the clock in the half court or you attack before their pressure is set with decisive north-south drives. BYU did the latter with paint attacks from Dybantsa and Rob Wright III. Houston tried to drag them into a low-possession fight, but Iowa State was comfortable there and won 70-67. So the wrong plan is to play medium pace and exchange live-ball mistakes; that feeds Iowa State. The better plan is extreme contrast: either attack instantly before the defense loads or grind them with size and shot-clock discipline so their steals cannot avalanche into scoring spurts. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401827693))

Position-by-position mismatch scan: at point guard, Lipsey is smaller at 6-1, so a big lead guard can shoot over him or post him if officiating allows contact; Dybantsa/BYU-style size creators are the clear stress point. At the 2/3, Iowa State has good size with Toure, Heise, and Nelson all 6-3 to 6-5, so they usually are not undersized there. At the 4, Jefferson at 6-9 and 240 is a real matchup problem for lighter forwards because he can bully switches and pass over help. Momcilovic at 6-8 is a different mismatch: not an above-the-rim 4, but a stretch forward who punishes slow closeouts and can force opposing bigs out of the lane. At the 5, Buchanan is 6-10 and Pleta is 6-11, but this is where truly dominant vertical athletes can challenge them most; Iowa State’s front line is solidly big, but not overwhelming above the rim. BYU’s first-half paint edge is the best named example that a powerful attack can still find interior leverage. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/2025-26))

Isolation vs team offense tendencies: the public evidence available supports a team-offense lean, not an iso-heavy attack. The strongest available numeric signal is 17.4 assists per game against 9.9 turnovers per game, plus game evidence showing assisted scoring chains through Jefferson, Lipsey, and Momcilovic in high-leverage games. I cannot verify a reliable public 2025-26 isolation-play percentage from a primary free source, so the honest scouting read is qualitative-but-evidenced: Iowa State relies more on shared creation than on repeated empty-side isolation. If you face them, loading up on one scorer is less useful than breaking their passing chain and shrinking the floor around Jefferson’s touches. ([foxsports.com](https://www.foxsports.com/college-basketball/iowa-state-cyclones-team-stats?utm_source=openai))

Transition offense and defense frequency: a precise possession-frequency split is not available from a verifiable public primary source here, but the results profile is still clear. Iowa State creates transition opportunities with 9.0 steals per game, and its defense is built to deny easy runouts by valuing the ball on offense with only 9.9 turnovers per game. That means they are functionally transition-positive on both ends: they generate live-ball offense and usually do not give much away. The practical counter is to send two to the offensive glass selectively against them only when Jefferson or Buchanan is occupied; otherwise prioritize floor balance and force them into half-court shot creation over length. ([foxsports.com](https://www.foxsports.com/college-basketball/iowa-state-cyclones-team-stats?utm_source=openai))

Coaching adaptability: T.J. Otzelberger’s staff has evidence of game-to-game and in-game adjustment quality. Iowa State beat Houston 70-67 in a game that required surviving shotmaking swings and finishing late. Three days after the BYU loss, the Cyclones answered with a 75-59 road win at Utah, getting 21 from Jefferson while Momcilovic hit four threes and broke the school single-season 3-point record. That sequence matters: they lost to a team that won the paint, then quickly stabilized and won on the road by leaning back into spacing and forward play. More recently, Iowa State also beat Texas Tech 75-53 in the Big 12 Tournament on March 12, 2026, another indicator that the staff can tighten the screws after a scouting prep window. Basketball is not a playoff series sport in college, but the available evidence says this staff does adjust across rematches and short turnarounds. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401827693))

Concrete game plan: To beat Iowa State you must do five specific things. One, play with a big initiator and attack the rim before their pressure loads; BYU’s 22-6 first-half paint edge and Dybantsa’s 29-10-9 line are the cleanest example. Two, do not feed their steal game with lazy slot passes; their 9.0 steals per game is a season-long warning. Three, make Jefferson a scorer rather than a hub by fronting elbow catches and bringing late help from non-shooters, because once he starts connecting actions the whole offense breathes. Four, top-lock Momcilovic and force him to put the ball on the deck into traffic instead of catching in rhythm from three. Five, win the rebounding/finishing battle; Iowa State can survive ugly games, as Houston learned in a 70-67 loss, but they are more vulnerable when the opponent turns the game into a size-and-paint contest, as BYU showed. In short: do not try to out-pressure Iowa State; out-size them at the point of attack, protect the ball, own the paint, and force them into a static half-court shotmaking game.
